Count what a ccp unit cell provides, then match the formula.
Y is in ccp (face-centred cubic), so per unit cell:
Y atoms = 8 corners × ⅛ + 6 faces × ½ = 1 + 3 = 4
A ccp lattice of N atoms provides N octahedral voids and 2N tetrahedral voids, so here:
octahedral voids = 4, tetrahedral voids = 8
The formula is XY₃, so for 4 atoms of Y there must be 4/3 atoms of X.
If X fills a fraction f of the octahedral voids:
4f = 4/3 ⇒ f = 1/3 = 33%
Check the alternative: if X filled tetrahedral voids, 8f = 4/3 would give f = 1/6 ≈ 17%, which
is not offered.
∴ X occupies 33% of the octahedral voids.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|46||0|0.s:
Take the reagents in order.
C₆H₅COOH + NH₃, then heat — the ammonium salt forms first and loses water on heating:
P = C₆H₅CONH₂, benzamide.
P + NaOBr — this is the Hoffmann bromamide degradation, which removes one carbon and
converts the amide to a primary amine:
Q = C₆H₅NH₂, aniline.
Q + conc. H₂SO₄, heated to 460 K — aniline first forms anilinium hydrogensulphate, and heating
to this temperature rearranges it to the para-substituted sulphonic acid:
R = p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid, sulphanilic acid.
Sulphanilic acid exists as a zwitterion, which is why it has such a high melting point and is
insoluble in organic solvents.
Note (1) sulphanilamide is the amide, not the acid, and needs a different route.
∴ R is sulphanilic acid.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|47||0|0:
Find the statement that is not correct.
(1) True — carbohydrates contain chiral carbons, so they rotate plane-polarised light. Glucose
is dextrorotatory, fructose laevorotatory.
(2) True — in lactose the C-1 of galactose is joined to the C-4 of glucose, a β-1,4 link.
(4) True — glucose pentaacetate has all five hydroxyls acetylated, which locks the ring shut.
The open-chain aldehyde form can no longer appear, so there is no carbonyl for hydroxylamine
to react with. This is one of the observations that showed glucose exists as a cyclic hemiacetal.
(3) False — aldoses and ketoses **do** isomerise in alkaline medium. Dilute base converts
glucose into a mixture of glucose, mannose and fructose through a common enediol intermediate.
This is the Lobry de Bruyn–van Ekenstein rearrangement, and it is exactly why fructose, a
ketose, still gives a positive Tollens' and Fehling's test: in alkali it rearranges to an aldose.
∴ statement (3) is not correct.
kcet|Chemistry|2014|49||0|0:
Find the statement that is not correct.
(1) True — solid PCl₅ is ionic, existing as the tetrahedral [PCl₄]⁺ and octahedral [PCl₆]⁻ ions.
It is covalent and trigonal bipyramidal only in the vapour.
(3) True — hypophosphorous acid, H₃PO₂, has two P–H bonds and is a strong reducing agent;
it reduces Ag⁺ to metallic silver.
(4) True — pure phosphine is not spontaneously inflammable. Ordinary samples catch fire in air
only because they are contaminated with traces of diphosphine, P₂H₄.
(2) False — the products are wrong. Phosphorous acid does disproportionate on heating, but it
gives **orthophosphoric** acid, not metaphosphoric acid:
4H₃PO₃ ⇒ 3H₃PO₄ + PH₃
Phosphorus goes from +3 to +5 in H₃PO₄ and down to −3 in PH₃, which is a proper
disproportionation; metaphosphoric acid, HPO₃, does not appear.
∴ statement (2) is not correct.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|50||0|0.s:
The question needs one ion that complexes with **both** reagents and one that complexes with
aqueous NaOH **only**.
Zn²⁺ — adding either reagent first precipitates white Zn(OH)₂, and then excess dissolves it:
with NaOH  Zn(OH)₂ + 2OH⁻ ⇒ [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻
with NH₃  Zn(OH)₂ + 4NH₃ ⇒ [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺
So zinc forms a complex with both ✓
Al³⁺ — with NaOH the amphoteric hydroxide dissolves:
Al(OH)₃ + OH⁻ ⇒ [Al(OH)₄]⁻
but with ammonia the Al(OH)₃ simply stays as a gelatinous precipitate; aluminium does not form
an ammine complex ✓ NaOH only
So the pair is Zn²⁺ and Al³⁺.
Cu²⁺ is ruled out because it forms the deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ but does **not** dissolve in
excess NaOH — the wrong way round. Pb²⁺ likewise complexes with NaOH only, so (3) has no ion
that works with both.
∴ Zn²⁺, Al³⁺.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|51||0|0.s:
Identify the gas first.
Y decolourises acidified KMnO₄, so Y is a reducing gas. Together with the fact that it comes
from a crystalline solid and dilute HCl, Y is sulphur dioxide:
Na₂SO₃ + 2HCl ⇒ 2NaCl + SO₂ + H₂O
So X = Na₂SO₃, sodium sulphite. (Na₂SO₄, offered in two options, is a sulphate and gives no
gas at all with dilute acid.)
SO₂ reducing permanganate:
5SO₂ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O ⇒ 5SO₄²⁻ + 2Mn²⁺ + 4H⁺ — the purple colour is discharged ✓
Now the second clue. Passing a gas Z into aqueous SO₂ gives colloidal sulphur, which is the
classic comproportionation of H₂S with SO₂:
2H₂S + SO₂ ⇒ 3S↓ + 2H₂O
Sulphur at −2 and at +4 meet in the middle at 0. The sulphur comes out so finely divided that
it forms a milky colloid.
∴ X is Na₂SO₃ and Z is H₂S.

kcet|Chemistry|2014|52||0|0.s:
The reaction identifies the type of amine, and then the formula fixes how many isomers there are.
A + NaNO₂/HCl at 0 °C gives benzyl alcohol and N₂. Nitrous acid converts an **aliphatic primary
amine** into an alcohol through an unstable diazonium salt that loses nitrogen at once:
C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ + HNO₂ ⇒ C₆H₅CH₂OH + N₂ + H₂O
So A is benzylamine — and C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ is indeed C₇H₉N ✓
Now count every aromatic amine of formula C₇H₉N:
1. benzylamine, C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ — primary, aliphatic –NH₂
2. N-methylaniline, C₆H₅NHCH₃ — secondary
3. o-toluidine, 2-CH₃C₆H₄NH₂
4. m-toluidine, 3-CH₃C₆H₄NH₂
5. p-toluidine, 4-CH₃C₆H₄NH₂
That is five. Only the first reacts as described, because the other four are either secondary
or aryl amines, whose diazonium salts are stable at 0 °C.
∴ 5 isomers.
